I was lucky to have a movie theater within biking distance of my house, The Inwood. In the spring of 1986, it began showing Terry Gilliam‘s science fiction-tinged, anti-fascist satire “Brazil” in one of its small upstairs theaters.
p

I knew the movie was inspired by George Orwell’s writings and real-life totalitarian governments, that Robert De Niro played a “repairman,” and that the previous year, 1985, Gilliam got into a spat with the releasing studio, Universal, over the movie’s sad but appropriate ending. (They warned him to cut it, but he refused; there’s a whole book about this battle if you’re interested.) Aside from that, I went in with no particular hope, except to see a fantasy as vividly imagined as Gilliam’s last film, “Time Bandits.”
p

“Brazil” cracked my teenage brain open. The instant the final credits rolled, I sprinted from the auditorium, bounded down the stairs, unchained my bike, and rode home as fast as I could, hoping to gather enough loose change from chairs and sofas to afford another ticket and zip back to the theater in time for the very next show. I made it.
p

If you’re reading this, you’ve probably seen “Brazil.” If not, see it, then come back here to read what I wrote about it. Try not to read anything else before, though. It’s so much fun to watch a film for the first time without knowing where it’ll go next.
p

What makes “Brazil” Gilliam’s best movie is the focused outrage that drives it. It’s astonishing how much propulsion a film can get from being directed by someone genuinely angry about the injustices he’s presenting. This movie is angry. It’s angry about the way governments, totalitarian and otherwise, let corrupt, stupid, sometimes deeply evil people hold positions of power. It’s angry about how agents of the state exploit and terrorize regular citizens for political reasons, for sport, for spite—or, in the case of the inciting event, because nobody will admit error.
p

The hero is Sam Lowry (Jonathan Pryce). With his sad smile and solitary ways, he’s a riff on Orwell’s battered hero Winston Smith. He just wants to do his job and get home to watch old movies on the telly. Then an accident involving a smashed bug and a teletype machine causes the wrong citizen to be kidnapped, hooded, and “disappeared” by masked police.
p

This sort of thing had happened, and was still happening, in lots of countries circa 1985-1986. It had happened in the USA to certain designated enemies of the state. Many citizens of Gilliam’s home country still viewed the film as a fantasy-infused warning or worst-case scenario, an account of things that happened elsewhere.
p

Nevertheless, in the mid-1980s, life under authoritarian rule was a common subject for movies. Why? Perhaps because it was the 40th anniversary of the end of World War II, which, we are told, the Good Guys won. Or maybe it was because Western nations like the United Kingdom and the United States had their own versions of “strongman” leaders (respectively, Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan). Whatever the explanation, “Brazil” played out in the same exhibition window as many other films about authoritarianism, including “Kiss of the Spider Woman,” “Salvador,” “Come and See,” “Eleni,” “When Father Was Away on Business,” and “The Assault.” If you wanted to be cheeky, you could add “The Color Purple” to the list.
p

Beyond its continuing relevance as a nightmare fantasy about how billions are forced to live, it is a stunningly complete work of production design by the late Norman Garwood, who also did “Time Bandits,” “The Princess Bride,” and “Hook.” The ductwork-of-no-apparent-purpose that winds through all the sets sums up the state’s stupid, pointless demands, as well as the reach of its surveillance efforts.
p

The ductwork is of a piece with the switchboard-and-wire-based phone system; the bizarrely tiny black-and-white video monitors that must be magnified with special lens attachments to become viewable; and the puny car Sam drives, which is so wrong for his tall frame that when he parks it and gets out, he seems to unfold from the driver’s seat. Everything seems wrong, somehow. It’s as if an entire society had been designed by a prideful man who keeps telling everyone he’s good with tools even though he plainly isn’t. Aesthetically, it’s one of the greatest films ever made.
p

Dramatically, not as much. The love story between Sam and “dream girl” Jill Layton, a beautiful female soldier in the revolutionary underground (Kim Griest), felt too abstract when the movie first came out and frankly still does. It’s obviously born out of the “pure-hearted hero fights for what’s right, gets girl as reward” screenwriting formula that was so popular in the 1980s, but that doesn’t excuse how dull it is. Critics at the time mostly blamed Greist.
p

The problem is that for all his visual and linguistic gifts, Gilliam has never cared much about women as people, only as plot elements. Notable exceptions, such as Madeline Stowe’s psychiatrist in “12 Monkeys” and Mercedes Ruehl and Amanda Plummer’s loyal partners in “The Fisher King,” can be attributed to differentiating factors, such as the screenwriters not being Terry Gilliam, and the actresses being resourceful enough to flesh out underwritten characters. Apparently Gilliam’s formidable co-writers, Tom Stoppard and Charles McKeown, couldn’t save the movie’s love story, or weren’t asked to. So blame should be assigned correctly.
p

The warmed-over Oedipal themes and jokes at the edges of “Brazil”—such as Jill’s look at the end conjuring a younger version of Sam’s rich, vain, plastic surgery-obsessed, bootlicking harpy of a mother (Katherine Helmond)—are mostly gross and sometimes baffling, and make the obligatory nature of the Sam-Jill relationship harder to excuse or ignore. That’s also on Gilliam.
p

Fortunately, there are major compensations, including an alternately rousing, intoxicating, and willfully naive score (by Michael Kamen), playful miniature cityscapes, lavish interior sets (many of which embellish pre-existing structures, such as the grain silo that got refurbished into a torture chamber); a refreshingly nasty approach to the presentation of violence (gore, screams); and minor characters so eccentric they might seem equally at home in books by Thomas Pynchon or Charles Dickens.
p

As Harry Tuttle, a “vigilante” duct repairman the government wants on suspicion of revolutionary activity, De Niro was cast against what was presumed to be his type at the time (antisocial, lethal, glum). He rappels through the concrete jungle like a blend of Batman and Tarzan—or a Wes Anderson character who somehow sprang into existence ten years before Anderson released “Bottle Rocket.”
p

Bob Hoskins and Derrick O’Connor play the government-employed “heating engineers” Spoor and Dowser, leering trolls who run a scam where they make duct problems even worse, then take bribes to make them tolerable again. Together with Ian Holm (as Sam’s fearful and incompetent boss) they epitomize the sorts of men who thrive in countries that prize loyalty over competence. Sheila Reed momentarily blows the doors off the film as Mrs. Buttle, the widow of the aforementioned wrong abductee, who emerges from her fog of grief to shriek at Sam, “What have you done with his BODY???”
p

Distill the story to one sentence, and it might go like this: “In a dictatorship where evil is never held accountable, a meek government worker risks his life to get justice for a man wrongly arrested by secret police.” That Sam had nothing to do with Mr. Buttle’s disappearance, and in fact went above and beyond by taking an interest in helping Mrs. Buttle, makes the central questions examined in “Brazil” resonate even more powerfully. What does it take to overcome people’s natural instinct for self-preservation, see strangers as people rather than numbers or concepts, and do the morally correct thing even when the law commands otherwise?
p

Forty-plus years after the original release of Gilliam’s magnum opus, sensible people know that fascism and its derivatives are not labels that magically appear when a nation fulfills a certain set of conditions, like speaking German and putting furnaces in prisons, but something more like a shake-and-bake recipe for violent domination and government-approved thievery that adapts to fit the personality of whatever culture hosts it. Ideology is a cover story, or a three-card-monte style distraction, from the real agenda, which is to create and maintain the type of society summed up by composer Frank Wilhoit, where “there are in-groups whom the law protects but does not bind, alongside out-groups whom the law binds but does not protect.”
p

Gilliam overreaches and oversteps a lot when crafting messages, but he’s spot on here. “Brazil” envisions the horrors that a supposed democracy can inflict on citizens when its leaders hold a monopoly on violence, and there are no co-branches or regulatory bodies with the ability (or courage) to step up and say no.
p

Some of the movie’s big set pieces and iconic images, especially ones involving sudden public bombings and tactical police crashing through windows and ceilings and carrying hooded prisoners off in canvas bags, feel like they could be a byproduct of Gilliam having moved from the US to England in the 1960s.
p

That was the period when American police were starting to treat white, upper-middle-class, college-educated protesters the way they had traditionally treated Blacks, Latinos, indigenous people, and other designated undesirables. Gilliam observed the return of authoritarianism in certain parts of Europe from a vantage point closer to home than his countrymen back in the States.
p

And of course, The Troubles in Northern Ireland were still going, and would continue as long as the British military was in charge. There were police with submachine guns, tanks with police logos, undercover disinformation campaigns, and jailhouse torture. “Not that long ago, Americans would regularly go to Northern Ireland to offer advice on reforming the region’s notoriously repressive policing,” wrote international law and human rights professor Martin S. Flaherty, in a 2020 article for Just Security. “Happily for Northern Ireland, and tragically for the United States, the lessons now run in the other direction.”
p

I thought about “Brazil” after seeing Jonathan Glazer’s unsparing Holocaust-era drama “Zone of Interest,” about the theory and practice of complicity. Complicity hinges on the ability to compartmentalize the moral and social implications of actions that should give any decent person nightmares. Michael Palin‘s character, Jack Lint, is Sam’s old friend who works in the Department of Information Retrieval. Which is to say, he tortures people.
p

It’s nothing personal, just a job he does for pay and benefits. The scene where Jack’s adorable son plays in his lush office during work hours while Jack has fresh blood on his smock sums up the cognitive dissonance required of workers in a terror state.
p

No wonder the goofy humor makes such chilling sense in context. Life in a country like this is inherently silly and surreal, but citizens have to pretend it’s sensible because if they complain, they could end up in prison or dead. It’s Abbott and Costello with jackboots. “Information Transit got the wrong man,” Jack says, torturing logic while he tortures Sam. “I got the right man. The wrong one was delivered to me as the right man; I accepted him in good faith as the right man. Was I wrong?”
p

The movie “doesn’t feel dated,” Gilliam told The Hollywood Reporter in a 40th-anniversary interview. “People keep coming up to me to say, ‘How did you understand the world was going to be like it is?’ And I say, ‘Well, you just had to keep your eyes open.’”
